In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis of a novel family of estradiol-platinum hybrid molecules and with the molecular modeling of three distinct families.
the development of new platinum(II) compounds with a high affinity for the estrogen receptor α and a potent antitumor activity.
the development of a new series of PEG-linked platinum(II)-hybrids with a high potential to be developed as anticancer drugs.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 16α- and 16β-estradioli-PEG-hybrid molecules are the most active compounds in the 3 families of 17-estradiol-PEG-hybride molecules reported in the present and our previous studies.
the most potent hybrids are those possessing a short alkyl chain at position 3 of the steroid nucleus and an alkyl tether between the steroid nucleus and the platinum(IV) core.
the 16β-alkyl-PEG-hybrid molecules are the most active and the 16α-alkyl- and 16α-ether-PEG-hydris are the least active.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the 16β position of the steroid nucleus is an ideal site for the attachment of a PEG chain.
the 16β-alkyl-PEG-estradiol hybrid series of molecules are the most promising among the three families of 17beta-estradiol-Pt(II) hybrids we have reported to date.
the length of the PEC chain and the orientation of its attachment on the steroid core do influence the activity of the hybrids.
